why.support: Betting ads are made very carefully. Every picture, sound and word is there to sell a feeling. Loot boxes in games do it too. When you can see the tricks, they work less.
why.core: Betting ads are some of the most carefully made texts you'll see. Every picture, sound and word is chosen to sell you a feeling, not just a bet. Loot boxes in games use a lot of the same tricks. Once you can see how they work, they lose their grip.
why.extend: Wagering ads are some of the most carefully built persuasive texts in Australian media. Images, sound, sequence and language link betting with belonging, skill and excitement. Loot boxes borrow the same design. Analysing them is a defence.

articles.title: How a betting ad works

body.support:
You must be **18** to bet in Australia. But sport is full of betting ads. They use **four tricks**.

1. **Mates.** Friends, footy and team colours. The ad says: betting is what fans like you do.
2. **Power words.** *Easy. In seconds. Back your knowledge.* These words make betting sound simple and smart.
3. **Sound and speed.** Fast music. A loud crowd. A slow-motion goal. You see the win. You never see the losses.
4. **Tiny print.** Ads must show a warning, like *Chances are you're about to lose.* Look how small and fast it is.

**Loot boxes** in games use tricks too. Bright flashes. Exciting sounds. The feeling that you *nearly* got the rare one.

The rules are changing. From **2027**, betting ads can't use famous sports stars or influencers.
body.core:
You have to be **18** to bet in Australia. But if you watch sport, you've seen hundreds of betting ads. They're built with great care, and they use the same **four tricks** again and again.

1. **Mates.** Friends on a couch, team colours, a big game. Researchers who studied 85 Australian betting ads found that **mateship** and **sports-fan rituals** were the most common ways ads tried to appeal to people. The message: betting is just what fans like you do.
2. **Power words.** *Easy. In seconds. Back your knowledge. You're in control.* These words make betting sound simple and smart, as if knowing your footy means you'll win.
3. **Sound and speed.** Fast music, a roaring crowd, a slow-motion goal, mates jumping up cheering. The **order** of the shots matters too: you see the win, but never the losses.
4. **Tiny print.** Since 2023, betting ads have had to show warnings like *Chances are you're about to lose* or *You win some. You lose more.* Look at how big, how fast and how late they appear.

**Loot boxes** in games use similar tricks: flashing lights, exciting sounds and the feeling that you *nearly* got the rare item. Since September 2024, new games in Australia with paid loot boxes get at least an **M** rating, and games with gambling you can play get **R 18+**.

The rules are changing. In 2023, a federal parliamentary inquiry said Australia should ban online gambling ads completely. That hasn't happened, but from **2027**, betting ads can't use famous sports stars, celebrities or influencers.
body.extend:
Gambling is legal only for adults in Australia, yet anyone who watches sport encounters a constant stream of wagering advertising. These ads are carefully constructed, and a few techniques recur.

1. **Mates.** A 2016 analysis of 85 Australian sports betting ads found that **mateship** and **sports-fan rituals** were the most common appeals, alongside winning, social status, thrill, and power and control. The effect is to **normalise** betting as part of being a fan.
2. **Power words.** The language of evaluation is turned up to full volume: *easy*, *in seconds*, *back your knowledge*. It frames betting as a skill you control, not a game of chance.
3. **Sound and speed.** Music, crowd noise, slow motion and editing shape your emotional response before you process a word. The **sequence** matters: the ad shows the win and skips the losses.
4. **Tiny print.** Since 2023, wagering ads must rotate warnings such as *Chances are you're about to lose*. How large, how long and where they appear changes how much they're noticed.

**Loot boxes** borrow the same design. Since September 2024, new games in Australia with paid loot boxes receive at least an **M** classification, and those with interactive simulated gambling, **R 18+**.

Regulation is contested. A 2023 parliamentary inquiry recommended a full ban on online gambling ads. The government chose narrower limits instead, including a ban, from 2027, on gambling ads featuring notable people such as athletes, celebrities and influencers.

caseStudies.title: Too young to bet, old enough to remember

body.support:
In 2018, researchers asked **111 young people** about betting ads. They were **11 to 16** years old. They were at basketball courts in Victoria.

- **81%** could name a betting brand.
- Many remembered the brands' **colours**.
- About **1 in 5** said they would bet when they turned 18.

None of them were old enough to bet. But they still remembered the ads.

That's how strong a good ad is. It sticks, even if it's not meant for you.
body.core:
In 2018, researchers surveyed **111 young people aged 11 to 16** at community basketball venues in Victoria. They asked what they remembered about sports betting ads.

- **81%** could name at least one betting brand.
- Many remembered details: the brands' **colours**, and the ways the ads tried to appeal to them.
- **About 1 in 5 (22.5%)** said they planned to bet when they turned 18. Boys were more likely to say this than girls.

None of these young people were allowed to bet. The ads were meant for adults. But the researchers found that the rules at the time didn't stop young people from seeing and remembering them.

That's the power of a well-made ad. You don't have to want it, or even be allowed it, for it to stick.
body.extend:
In 2018, a research team led by Nyemcsok surveyed **111 young people aged 11 to 16** at community basketball venues in Victoria. They asked what the young people remembered about sports betting ads, and what they thought of them.

- **81.1%** could name at least one sports betting brand.
- Many knew the brands' distinctive features, such as their **colours**, and the **appeal strategies** the ads used.
- **22.5%** said they planned to bet on sport at 18. Boys were much more likely to say so than girls.

The authors concluded that the rules at the time didn't seem to work. They weren't stopping young people from seeing and remembering gambling ads.

The study raises a question about audience. A text can be aimed at one group (adult sports fans) and still reach another group powerfully: their younger brothers, sisters and kids.

source.name: Nyemcsok and others (2018), “Young people's recall and perceptions of gambling advertising and intentions to gamble on sport”, Journal of Behavioral Addictions

teacher.overview: Students analyse how sports betting ads and loot boxes persuade: appeals to mateship and fandom, forceful evaluative language, and the use of images, sound and sequence (what's large, what's heard, what's shown and what's left out). They separate objective from subjective language, study a real Victorian study of young people's recall of betting brands, and storyboard an honest counter-ad for Year 7 students. The course includes current Australian rules: mandatory warning taglines (2023), loot box classification (2024) and the ban on notable people in gambling ads (from 2027).
prep: Choose **one or two current betting ads** (TV or the brands' official video channels) to show in class, and a game with paid loot boxes (video clip of an opening, not a live purchase). Watch them first. Rules change from 2027, so newer ads will look different.
Don't ask students to visit betting sites or apps.
Check your school's wellbeing team knows the course is running, in case it prompts a disclosure.
Print the storyboard page on A3 if you can.

teacher.answers:
**Four tricks:** mates, power words, sound and speed, tiny print.

**Ad script:** 1 mates (belonging, betting is what fans do); 2 sound (excitement); 3 power words (betting sounds like skill and easy); 4 framing (the phone and odds are the most important thing); 5 sequence (shows the win, never the loss); 6 tiny print (the warning is easy to miss).

**Fact or feeling:** feel the rush — feeling; 18 or over — fact; best odds — opinion; odds board — fact; better with a bet — opinion; loot box rating — fact.

**Turn it down (samples):** You can place a bet quickly, which also makes it easy to lose money quickly. / Knowing your footy doesn't stop you losing; results come down to chance. / You don't need to bet to enjoy the game.

**Case study:** brands, colours and appeal strategies; meant for adults, but seen by young people at home and at sport; repetition, sport, colours and humour make them memorable.

realityCheck: **Some students live with gambling harm.** A parent, sibling or the student themselves may gamble. Never ask students to share their own or their family's betting. Keep the focus on the ads. Gambler's Help Youthline (under 25) is **1800 262 376**, 24/7; the statewide Gambler's Help line is **1800 858 858**.
**Loot boxes are personal.** Many students buy them. Avoid shaming; analyse the design, not the buyer.
**Choose the ads yourself.** Use official ads from TV or the brands' video channels, watched beforehand. Don't send students to betting sites or apps.
**The rules are moving.** From 2027, ads can't use notable people, so the ads you show may change. That's a good discussion in itself: what will the ads use instead?
**Works in a real class:** yes. Footy and gaming fans are often the most engaged; they know these ads by heart. The honest-ad storyboard can become a short film for younger students.
